title: Historiography Manifest for the Barton Bernstein Offline Print Packet
scope: Publicly locatable historiographical and interpretive pieces on NATO expansion, the Clinton administration decision process, the 1990 non-extension-assurances debate, Russia-related constraint, and the post-Cold War European security order.
printPolicy: The public repository stores citations, official URLs, page counts, and build scripts.
Full article PDFs are assembled only into an ignored local print packet under private/.
The user-provided Project MUSE PDF is included only from the local attached file path.
Paywalled, access-controlled, or web-only copyrighted pieces are listed with citation notes and short relevance summaries rather than reproduced in full.

primaryDocumentPackage.title: Clinton NATO Expansion Bernstein 1000-Page Primary Document Package
primaryDocumentPackage.description: The already assembled local primary-document package selected from the public manifest.

includedFullText.title: The U.S. Decision to Enlarge NATO: How, When, Why, and What Next?
includedFullText.citation: James M. Goldgeier, "The U.S. Decision to Enlarge NATO: How, When, Why, and What Next?," Brookings, June 1, 1999.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: A concise statement by the author of the core monograph on how the Clinton administration moved from uncertainty to a first-round enlargement decision.

includedFullText.title: Bill and Boris: A Window Into a Most Important Post-Cold War Relationship
includedFullText.citation: James Goldgeier, "Bill and Boris: A Window Into a Most Important Post-Cold War Relationship," Texas National Security Review, 2018.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: Uses newly released Clinton-Yeltsin records to foreground meeting records, memory, and the problem of reconstructing presidential diplomacy around NATO enlargement.

includedFullText.authors: James Goldgeier and Joshua R. Itzkowitz Shifrinson
includedFullText.title: Evaluating NATO Enlargement: Scholarly Debates, Policy Implications, and Roads Not Taken
includedFullText.citation: James Goldgeier and Joshua R. Itzkowitz Shifrinson, "Evaluating NATO enlargement: scholarly debates, policy implications, and roads not taken," International Politics 57 (2020): 291-321.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: The best compact map of the major scholarly debates, counterfactuals, and roads not taken after the enlargement decision.

includedFullText.title: Deal or No Deal? The End of the Cold War and the U.S. Offer to Limit NATO Expansion
includedFullText.citation: Joshua R. Itzkowitz Shifrinson, "Deal or No Deal? The End of the Cold War and the U.S. Offer to Limit NATO Expansion," International Security 40, no. 4 (Spring 2016): 7-44.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: A central revisionist article on the 1990 assurances question, useful as a foil for Kramer, Sarotte, and Trachtenberg.

includedFullText.title: NATO Enlargement and U.S. Foreign Policy: The Origins, Durability, and Impact of an Idea
includedFullText.citation: Joshua R. Itzkowitz Shifrinson, "NATO enlargement and U.S. foreign policy: the origins, durability, and impact of an idea," International Politics 57 (2020): 342-370.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: Explains how enlargement became a durable U.S. policy idea after initial debate, which pairs directly with the Clinton-era primary documents.

includedFullText.title: Eastbound and Down: The United States, NATO Enlargement, and Suppressing the Soviet and Western European Alternatives, 1990-1992
includedFullText.citation: Joshua R. Itzkowitz Shifrinson, "Eastbound and down: The United States, NATO enlargement, and suppressing the Soviet and Western European alternatives, 1990-1992," Journal of Strategic Studies 43, nos. 6-7 (2020): 816-846.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: Pushes the origins story back into 1990-1992 and is important for distinguishing Bush-era structuring choices from Clinton-era enlargement decisions.

includedFullText.title: The Myth of a No-NATO-Enlargement Pledge to Russia
includedFullText.citation: Mark Kramer, "The Myth of a No-NATO-Enlargement Pledge to Russia," The Washington Quarterly 32, no. 2 (April 2009): 39-61.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: The classic skeptical account of the no-pledge claim, essential beside Shifrinson and Trachtenberg.

includedFullText.title: How to Enlarge NATO: The Debate inside the Clinton Administration, 1993-95
includedFullText.citation: M.E. Sarotte, "How to Enlarge NATO: The Debate inside the Clinton Administration, 1993-95," International Security 44, no. 1 (Summer 2019): 7-41.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: Directly reconstructs the Clinton administration debate over the speed and form of enlargement, making it the closest historiographical companion to the v2 primary-document core.

includedFullText.title: The United States and the NATO Non-extension Assurances of 1990: New Light on an Old Problem?
includedFullText.citation: Marc Trachtenberg, "The United States and the NATO Non-extension Assurances of 1990: New Light on an Old Problem?," International Security 45, no. 3 (Winter 2020/21): 162-203.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: The attached article belongs in the offline packet because it gives Barton the most detailed statement of the non-extension-assurances debate in a form already supplied by the user.

includedFullText.title: The United States and the NATO Non-extension Assurances of 1990: New Light on an Old Problem? (Longer Footnoted Version)
includedFullText.citation: Marc Trachtenberg, longer footnoted version of "The United States and the NATO Non-extension Assurances of 1990," UCLA faculty site.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: The article itself points readers to this longer and more fully footnoted version, so it is useful for a print-only reader.

includedFullText.authors: James Goldgeier, Joshua R. Itzkowitz Shifrinson, Paul van Hooft, Stefanie von Hlatky, Michel Fortmann, Alexander Lanoszka, Kimberly Marten, Rajan Menon, and Sara Bjerg Moller
includedFullText.title: NATO Expansion in Retrospect
includedFullText.citation: H-Diplo/ISSF Policy Roundtable XII-1, "NATO Expansion in Retrospect," October 19, 2020.
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: A compact, printable roundtable with Goldgeier and Shifrinson framing the issue and multiple scholars disagreeing over enlargement's consequences.

includedFullText.authors: Daniel S. Hamilton and Kristina Spohr, editors
includedFullText.title: Open Door: NATO and Euro-Atlantic Security After the Cold War
includedFullText.citation: Daniel S. Hamilton and Kristina Spohr, eds., Open Door: NATO and Euro-Atlantic Security After the Cold War (Washington, DC: Center for Transatlantic Relations, 2019).
includedFullText.whyForBernstein: Large but valuable as a printed reference: it combines participant reflections and scholarship on NATO's open-door policy, Clinton-era enlargement, and the post-Cold War security architecture.
